title: Orbital Launch Vehicle Team
brief: A 3D-printed wiring channel for the forward closure of a two-stage rocket, designed so the drogue chute cannot snag on it.

facts.label: printed assembly: body, connector insert, plate

did: Designed the wiring channel from scratch: channel body with heat-set inserts, removable Molex insert, screw-down plate
Shaped the channel and connector seating so the parachute has nothing to catch on at deployment
Refined the sustainer and booster bulkheads for tolerancing and friction fits
Laser cut bulkheads and wet sanded the carbon fiber body tubes
summary: Structures work on the team's two-stage rocket. I designed the 3D-printed wiring channel in the forward closure from scratch: a channel body with heat-set threaded inserts, a removable insert that holds the Molex connectors, and a screw-down plate. The connectors let the motor section and the flash bay separate so the drogue chute can deploy at apogee, and the main design challenge was making sure the parachute couldn't catch on the connectors or the channel itself. I also refined the sustainer and booster bulkheads for tolerancing and friction fits, laser cut bulkheads, wet sanded carbon fiber body tubes, and helped with general assembly.

summary: A mini-ITX machine designed from the case outward. I came into the project wanting to design for FDM manufacturing first, with as little support material as possible, so the enclosure, the rear I/O bracket and the dual-fan GPU shroud are all shaped to come off the bed clean. Getting a 240 mm AIO, a modular PSU and a PCIe riser into that volume meant working the compatibility, airflow and cable routing problems in CAD first.

title: FDM Printer Modding
brief: An i3-style printer rebuilt with linear rails, a new toolhead and Klipper, taking print acceleration from 80 to over 300 mm/s².
did: Swapped the X and Y axes to linear rails and upgraded the belts
Built a new toolhead with a custom part cooling shroud
Wired a bed probe into the toolhead breakout board
Flashed Klipper, hosted it on a Raspberry Pi, and tuned acceleration, jerk and input shaping
summary: The machines that produce parts for everything else on this page, rebuilt to keep up. On the i3-style printer that meant swapping to linear rails on both the X and Y axes, upgraded belts and a new toolhead, a custom fan shroud for part cooling, a bed probe wired into the toolhead breakout, and Klipper flashed and hosted on a Raspberry Pi so acceleration, jerk and input shaping could actually be tuned. Print acceleration went from 80 to over 300 mm/s².

summary: A personal assistant I text like a person. A small Python bot takes each message, answers the quick things itself, and hands longer jobs to a few specialized AI agents, each on the cheapest model that can do the job, with a spending cap on every job and on the day. It also runs things on a schedule, and it can save a job that took a lot of steps as a skill for next time. Emails only send after my yes. The link goes to its dashboard, which shows how it is built and a few live numbers.
